domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m ≥ 2 (so m-1 ≥ 1 and the tuple length is at least 1)
g is an integer with g ≥ 0
x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) has each x_k a positive integer (x_k ∈ {1,2,3,...})
Constraints are conditional on the comparison between i+j and m:
• If i+j < m then the inequality x_i + x_j ≥ x_{i+j} is required (here i+j ∈ {2,...,m-1}, so x_{i+j} is a valid component)
• If i+j > m then the inequality x_i + x_j + 1 ≥ x_{i+j-m} is required (here i+j-m ∈ {1,...,m-2}, so x_{i+j-m} is a valid component)
• If i+j = m then no inequality is specified by the definition
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every fixed integers m and g with m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0, let K_{m,g} be the set of all tuples x ∈ Z_{>0}^{m-1} such that Σ_{k=1}^{m-1} x_k = g and for all i,j ∈ {1,...,m-1}: if i+j<m then x_i+x_j ≥ x_{i+j}, and if i+j>m then x_i+x_j+1 ≥ x_{i+j-m}. Then K_{m,g} is finite.

shared_context.statement_nl: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m, g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m, g) <= N(m, g + 1).

payload.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Then K_{m,g} is a finite set.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Fix integers m and g with m >= 2 and g >= 0, and define K_{m,g} as in the statement.

We will show that K_{m,g} is finite.

Let x = (x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}) be any element of K_{m,g}. By definition, each x_k is a positive integer, so for every k in {1,\dots,m-1} we have
x_k >= 1.
Also, again by definition,
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = g.

From positivity and the fixed sum g, each coordinate is automatically bounded above by g: indeed, for any k,
x_k <= x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} = g.
So every x in K_{m,g} satisfies
x \in \{1,2,\dots,g\}^{m-1}
when g >= 1.
Therefore K_{m,g} is a subset of the finite set \{1,2,\dots,g\}^{m-1}, hence K_{m,g} is finite.

It remains only to consider the case g = 0. If x were in K_{m,0}, then each x_k would be a positive integer, so
x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} >= m-1.
Since m >= 2, we have m-1 >= 1, so x_1 + \cdots + x_{m-1} >= 1, which cannot equal 0. Hence K_{m,0} = \varnothing, and therefore K_{m,0} is finite.

Thus in all cases K_{m,g} is finite.

Note that the inequalities involving i and j are irrelevant for this finiteness argument: the positivity of the coordinates together with the fixed sum already places K_{m,g} inside a finite ambient set.
result_payload.proof_summary: Any tuple in K_{m,g} has m-1 positive integer coordinates summing to g, so each coordinate lies between 1 and g when g>=1; hence K_{m,g} is contained in the finite set {1,...,g}^{m-1}. If g=0, no such positive tuple exists, so K_{m,g} is empty. Therefore K_{m,g} is finite.

used_external_facts: A finite Cartesian product of finite sets is finite.
Any subset of a finite set is finite.
